title: Bandwidth-Fair Token Orchestrator for Tensor-Pipeline Coordination
creator: Marcus Chen
description:
Problem summary:

Current tensor/pipeline multi-GPU scheduling tries to maximize kernel execution overlap with NCCL collectives by heuristics tied to static device topology assumptions. This often leads to: skewed bandwidth utilization across heterogeneous nodes, tail latency spikes during prefill->decode transitions, and suboptimal kernel selection when attention windows vary per-request. We need a scheduler that is aware of per-GPU bandwidth budgets, token-level criticality (prefill tokens vs decode tokens), and can allocate NCCL windows dynamically to reduce stalls while preserving latency SLOs.

Proposed solution overview:

Implement a Bandwidth-Fair Token Orchestrator (BFTO) sitting in the runtime rendezvous layer that: (1) maintains per-GPU transient bandwidth tokens updated from NIC/GPU telemetry and NCCL progress hooks, (2) classifies in-flight work units (microbatches/prefill shards/decode shards) by criticality and expected comm pattern, (3) computes windowed NCCL reservation slots that are comm-overlapped with kernels predicted by the kernel-selection hinting system, and (4) enforces graceful backpressure and fallback to single-GPU decode when cross-device budgets are constrained. The BFTO will integrate with existing kernel hints produced by the kernel selector and with the KV cache prefix-awareness mechanism.

Key design details:

- Bandwidth accounting: each GPU maintains a sliding-window estimate of available NCCL bandwidth (bytes/sec) derived from NIC counters and NCCL time-slices. We smooth with EWMA and expose a lightweight API for the orchestrator.
- Token model: bandwidth tokens are issued per scheduling epoch (configurable, default 5ms). Tokens represent transferable bytes of collective traffic that a stage can consume when it initiates an all-reduce/all-gather.
- Criticality scoring: incoming requests are scored by (phase: prefill vs decode), sequence length, and latency policy (SLO tier). Prefill shards get lower criticality for throughput-optimized jobs; decode shards are prioritized for latency-sensitive tokens. Scores adjust reservation windows.
- Window allocation algorithm: greedy, proportional-share allocator that attempts to maximize kernel-NCCL overlap by selecting windows sized to expected collective duration (estimated from model sharding metadata and microbatch size). When budgets insufficient, BFTO reduces window sizes or shifts NCCL to later non-critical windows.
- Kernel hinting integration: kernel selector provides predicted kernel durations and memory bandwidth estimates per operation. BFTO uses these to align NCCL start times such that collective traffic overlaps compute-heavy kernels on other stages.
- Fallbacks: if overlap fails or bandwidth drops below safety threshold, the orchestrator triggers staged fallbacks: 1) compress collective (FP16/quantized comm), 2) increase async rendezvous spacing, 3) route to a local-only decode variant.

Observability and metrics:

We will add BFTO-specific metrics: per-GPU bandwidth_token_rate, window_allocations_per_epoch, collisions (failed overlap attempts), prefill_tail_latency_99.9, decode_tail_latency_99.9, and rollback_count. Dashboards will compare before/after for key workloads.

Rollout plan:

1) Unit tests + microbench harness exercising synthetic NCCL emulation (target: 1 week)
2) Canary on dedicated staging cluster with homogeneous GPUs (2 nodes) — compare throughput/latency to baseline (2 weeks)
3) Heterogeneous cluster canary with attenuation toggles (1 week)
4) Gradual production rollouts behind runtime feature flag (50% traffic -> 100%) with automatic rollback on SLO breach

Trade-offs and alternatives considered:

- Centralized scheduler vs local per-rendezvous orchestrator: chose local rendezvous-level BFTO to reduce cross-node coordination latency and to limit single-point-of-failure blast radius.
- Strict bandwidth reservation vs opportunistic stealing: opportunistic stealing yields higher throughput but complicates tail guarantees; BFTO uses conservative reservation with limited optimistic stealing heuristics.
- Kernel fusion to avoid some collectives: high implementation cost and model-dependent benefits; deferred to later optimization phase.

Open questions / unknowns:

- Accuracy of collective duration estimates for heavily quantized kernels across different GPUs. Need microbench data.
- How fast can NIC-derived bandwidth estimates react to transient contention?
- Interplay with existing autoscaler policies—will BFTO's backpressure interact poorly with node autoscaling?

Acceptance criteria:

- BFTO integrates with kernel selector and can produce window allocations within 1ms of rendezvous lifecycle start.
- For target gen workloads (400-token prefill, 1-token decode), 99.9th percentile decode latency improves by at least 15% on heterogeneous 4-GPU clusters.
- No more than 2% throughput regression for high-throughput batch-prefill workloads.
- Dashboards and alerts surface window allocation failures and trigger automatic rollback when decode 99.9 exceeds SLO by 20%.

Testing plan:

- Microbench: simulate variable collective sizes and validate allocator properties (fairness, bounded starvation).
- Integration: end-to-end with runtime harness using real NCCL on staging hardware, compare with baseline metrics.
- Loadtest: synthetic PLG traffic reproduction to validate regressions under load.

Implementation milestones / tasks:

- Task 1: instrumentation library for per-GPU bandwidth estimate and NCCL hooks (ENG)
- Task 2: BFTO core allocator and policy engine (ENG)
- Task 3: kernel-selector hook integration and hint schema extension (ENG)
- Task 4: KV-cache prefix alignment and reservation tests (ENG)
- Task 5: dashboards, alerts, and rollout automation (SRE/Console)

Expected risks and mitigations:

- Risk: bandwidth estimates lag real contention -> mitigation: conservative smoothing, quick failover to fallback policies.
- Risk: increased scheduler complexity causes regressions -> mitigation: unit tests + staged rollouts + runtime feature flag with safe defaults.
